findings.assertion: The Centro Urbano Presidente Alemán was authorized in July 1947 and inaugurated on 2 September 1949 as a state-supported high-density housing project; the 1999 oral-history study provides this exact inauguration date.
findings.source_locator: de Garay 1999, p.74 note 1 (web lines 40-41); Noelle 2021 HTML lines 74-77
findings.limitations: Exact inaugural day from one secondary source; original government decree and opening program unseen.

findings.assertion: The construction predates ISSSTE: the earlier public-pensions institution financed/planned federal worker housing, while ISSSTE only came into being under the law published 30 December 1959. De Garay's footnote retroactively calls the initial administrator ISSSTE and must not be copied without chronology correction.
findings.source_locator: de Garay 1999, p.74 note 1; ISSSTE institutional history (14 Jan 2020)
findings.limitations: Exact 1947 legal title, tenancy agreement and transfer dates need primary Pensiones documents; this is a demonstrable anachronism warning.

findings.assertion: The multifamiliar model concentrated apartments and services in a landscaped superblock, explicitly testing the Modern Movement's separation of pedestrian greenspace from vehicular circulation and the state's replacement of single-lot housing with collective development.
findings.source_locator: de Garay 1999, pp.73-76; Sánchez Rueda 2009/2017, direct abstract lines 36-39
findings.limitations: Modernist design intentions should not be mistaken for evidence of actual resident outcomes.

findings.assertion: De Garay's published history of CUPA draws on 60 semi-structured interviews with inhabitants; quoted residents recount opposition and rumors that moving to the project would restrict their ability to leave at night. The testimonies document residents' recollections, not verified press campaigns.
findings.source_locator: de Garay 1999, pp.76-77 (web lines 59-101), especially oral accounts attributed to María Romero and Rosa Zaragoza
findings.limitations: Original audio recordings, interview selection and contemporary newspapers not independently reviewed; no claim that rumors were actually enforced.

findings.assertion: De Garay states the project was initially offered at moderate rent to public employees, later moving toward condominium ownership after the 1985 earthquake. The precise legal transfer sequence remains to be established from property and agency records.
findings.source_locator: de Garay 1999, p.74 note 1; SOSBrutalism preservation description, updated 2026
findings.limitations: The 1985 trigger, transfer timing, and responsible institution are secondary-source assertions, not verified deeds or legislation.

findings.assertion: At the CUPA street perimeter, de Garay describes five tall connected wings forming a diagonal zigzag from Félix Cuevas toward Parroquia, with other tall blocks away from that diagonal; this shape is the feature to explain from a lawful public vantage.
geographies: Félix Cuevas / Parroquia, Colonia del Valle
findings.limitations: Number of separate tall buildings disputed by sources (seven in de Garay; six in SOSBrutalism); original floor plan and safe public vantage not verified.

findings.assertion: The complex's original ground-floor program combined shops, covered circulation, collective laundry, administrative offices, a dispensary and meeting space. These explain how modernist housing bundled domestic and civic services rather than merely stacking apartments.
findings.limitations: Description of original program only; which facilities remain today, access and privacy require verification.

findings.assertion: The prototype CUPA apartment split living functions across two levels: a small kitchen/breakfast area on one level, connected by an interior stair to bath, storage and adaptable room space. The published sizes span approximately 48 to 79 square meters.
findings.limitations: No private apartment interiors may be presented as open visitor attractions; verify plan types against original drawings.

findings.assertion: The 1952 Centro Urbano Presidente Juárez offers a counterpoint to CUPA: the ICAA/MFAH catalog of Mathias Goeritz's 1952 article identifies Mario Pani and Enrique del Moral as architectural collaborators and Carlos Mérida's art as integral to the design, not applied decoration.
geographies: Centro Urbano Presidente Juárez / Colonia Roma
findings.source_locator: ICAA/MFAH ICAA Record 735979 synopsis and original citation, Arquitectura no.8 (Dec 1952) pp.419-425; Gómez Porter 2017 INAH abstract
findings.limitations: The original Goeritz article is behind login; surviving portions of the housing site and any murals have not been field-verified. Do not plan entry into residences.

findings.assertion: The CUPA high-rise count is not safely normalized: de Garay's 1999 architectural description reports seven high blocks and six low, whereas a heritage catalog updated in 2026 reports six tall blocks and six low. Record a documented source disagreement instead of choosing one count.
findings.source_locator: de Garay 1999 p.74 lines 35-37; SOSBrutalism catalog object 18861206
findings.limitations: Possible counting conventions differ for connected wings; require a signed original plan/numbered elevations before adjudication.

findings.assertion: Docomomo's scholarly abstract states Pani invited José Clemente Orozco to begin a mural on a specially designed undulating wall at CUPA. This must remain an archival art-history lead, not a claim that an accessible or surviving mural can be seen.
findings.source_locator: Noelle 2021, Docomomo Journal 65 pp.16-21, HTML abstract lines 75-77; bibliography identifies Arquitectura/México no.30 (Feb 1950)
findings.limitations: Original mural designs, completion status, preservation, imagery and rights not established; do not create a photo toggle.
